content.value: CI/CD is the practice of automating the entire software delivery process — from the moment a developer pushes code to the moment it's running in production. It's like an assembly line in a factory: code automatically goes through building, testing, and deploying without any manual steps.

content.title: CI/CD Pipeline Flow
content.value:
graph LR
    A["👨‍💻 Developer\ngit push"] --> B["🔨 Build\nCompile code"]
    B --> C["🧪 Test\nUnit + Integration"]
    C --> D["📦 Package\nDocker image"]
    D --> E["🚀 Deploy Staging\nTest environment"]
    E --> F["✅ Deploy Production\nLive users"]
    style A fill:#1a2332,stroke:#00d4ff,color:#e2e8f0
    style B fill:#1a2332,stroke:#f59e0b,color:#e2e8f0
    style C fill:#1a2332,stroke:#10b981,color:#e2e8f0
    style D fill:#1a2332,stroke:#8b5cf6,color:#e2e8f0
    style E fill:#1a2332,stroke:#ef4444,color:#e2e8f0
    style F fill:#1a2332,stroke:#00d4ff,color:#e2e8f0

**Continuous Integration (CI)** — Automatically build and test code every time someone pushes a commit. Catch bugs within minutes, not days.

**Continuous Delivery (CD)** — Automatically prepare releases that are ready to deploy at the push of a button.

**Continuous Deployment** — Go one step further: automatically deploy every change to production with no human intervention.
Without CI/CD, a team might deploy once a month with a scary 'big bang' release. With CI/CD, teams deploy multiple times per day with confidence — each change is small, tested, and easy to roll back.

quiz.question: What is the difference between Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment?
options: Delivery requires manual approval to deploy; Deployment is fully automatic
Delivery is for staging; Deployment is for production
quiz.explanation: Continuous Delivery prepares releases that are ready to deploy but requires a human to click 'Deploy'. Continuous Deployment automatically pushes every change to production with no manual step.

content.value: **GitHub Actions** is GitHub's built-in CI/CD platform. Pipelines are defined as YAML files in `.github/workflows/` in your repository. Every push, pull request, or schedule can trigger a workflow.

content.title: Your First GitHub Actions Workflow
content.value:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI Pipeline

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  build-and-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    
    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
      
      - name: Setup Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '18'
          cache: 'npm'
      
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci
      
      - name: Run linter
        run: npm run lint
      
      - name: Run tests
        run: npm test
      
      - name: Build
        run: npm run build
Use 'actions/checkout@v4' to clone your repo, 'actions/setup-node@v4' to install Node.js with caching. The 'cache: npm' option caches node_modules between runs, speeding up builds significantly.

quiz.question: Where do GitHub Actions workflow files live in a repository?
quiz.explanation: GitHub Actions automatically discovers and runs workflow YAML files stored in the .github/workflows/ directory of your repository.

content.value: A well-designed pipeline has distinct stages that act as quality gates. Code must pass each stage before moving to the next. If any stage fails, the pipeline stops and the developer is notified.

content.title: Multi-Stage Pipeline with Docker
content.value:
name: Full CI/CD Pipeline

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '18' }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test

  build:
    needs: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Build Docker image
        run: docker build -t myapp:${{ github.sha }} .
      - name: Push to registry
        run: |
          echo ${{ secrets.DOCKER_PASSWORD }} | docker login -u ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }} --password-stdin
          docker push myapp:${{ github.sha }}

  deploy:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    steps:
      - name: Deploy to production
        run: |
          echo "Deploying version ${{ github.sha }} to production..."
The 'needs' keyword creates dependencies between jobs. 'deploy needs: build' means deploy only runs after build succeeds. The 'if' condition ensures deploy only runs on the main branch, not on PRs.

quiz.question: What does 'needs: test' mean in a GitHub Actions job?
options: The job only runs after the 'test' job completes successfully
The job runs in parallel with tests
quiz.explanation: 'needs: test' creates a dependency — the current job waits for the 'test' job to finish successfully before starting. If 'test' fails, this job is skipped.

content.value: Testing is the backbone of CI/CD. Without automated tests, you're just automatically deploying bugs faster. The **testing pyramid** shows the optimal distribution of test types.

content.title: Testing Pyramid
content.value:
graph TB
    E2E["🔝 E2E Tests\n(Few, slow, expensive)\nBrowser automation, full user flows"] 
    INT["🔷 Integration Tests\n(Medium count)\nAPI endpoints, database queries"]
    UNIT["🟢 Unit Tests\n(Many, fast, cheap)\nIndividual functions & components"]
    style E2E fill:#1a2332,stroke:#ef4444,color:#e2e8f0
    style INT fill:#1a2332,stroke:#f59e0b,color:#e2e8f0
    style UNIT fill:#1a2332,stroke:#10b981,color:#e2e8f0

**Unit Tests** — Test individual functions in isolation. Fast (milliseconds each). Run on every commit. Example: testing a `calculateDiscount()` function.

**Integration Tests** — Test how components work together. Example: testing that your API endpoint correctly reads from the database.

**End-to-End (E2E) Tests** — Test the entire user flow in a real browser. Slow but catch real-world issues. Example: testing the full checkout flow.

content.title: Testing Matrix (Multiple Node Versions)
content.value:
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        node-version: [16, 18, 20]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node-version }}
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test
      - name: Upload coverage
        uses: codecov/codecov-action@v3
        if: matrix.node-version == 18
Strategy matrix runs the same job with different configurations in parallel. Testing against Node 16, 18, and 20 simultaneously ensures your app works across all supported versions.

quiz.question: According to the testing pyramid, which type of test should you have the most of?
quiz.explanation: Unit tests form the base of the pyramid — they're fast, cheap, and you should have many of them. Integration tests are in the middle. E2E tests at the top should be few and focused on critical paths.

content.title: Using Secrets in GitHub Actions
content.value:
# Store secrets in: Settings → Secrets → Actions

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production       # Links to GitHub Environment
    steps:
      - name: Deploy to AWS
        env:
          AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: ${{ secrets.AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID }}
          AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: ${{ secrets.AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY }}
        run: |
          aws ecs update-service --cluster prod --service api --force-new-deployment
      
      - name: Notify Slack
        run: |
          curl -X POST ${{ secrets.SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL }} \
            -d '{"text": "✅ Deployed to production!"}'
Never echo, print, or log secrets in your pipeline! GitHub masks known secrets in logs, but custom formatting can accidentally expose them. Always use the ${{ secrets.NAME }} syntax — never hardcode.

quiz.question: Where should production API keys be stored in a CI/CD pipeline?
options: In the CI/CD platform's encrypted secrets store
quiz.explanation: Secrets must be stored in the CI/CD platform's encrypted secrets store (e.g., GitHub Secrets, GitLab CI Variables). They are injected at runtime and masked in logs.

content.value: How you deploy matters as much as what you deploy. Different strategies offer different tradeoffs between risk, speed, and complexity.

content.title: Deployment Strategies Comparison
content.value:
graph TD
    subgraph RR ["Rolling Update"]
        R1["v1 v1 v1"] --> R2["v2 v1 v1"] --> R3["v2 v2 v1"] --> R4["v2 v2 v2"]
    end
    subgraph BG ["Blue-Green"]
        B1["Blue (v1) LIVE"] --> B2["Green (v2) Ready"]
        B2 --> B3["Switch traffic → Green LIVE"]
    end
    subgraph CN ["Canary"]
        C1["v1 (90% traffic)"] --> C2["v2 (10% traffic)"]
        C2 --> C3["v2 (100% traffic)"]
    end
    style RR fill:#0f1923,stroke:#00d4ff33,color:#e2e8f0
    style BG fill:#0f1923,stroke:#10b98133,color:#e2e8f0
    style CN fill:#0f1923,stroke:#f59e0b33,color:#e2e8f0

**Rolling Update** — Replace instances one by one. Zero downtime. Default in Kubernetes.

**Blue-Green** — Run two identical environments. Switch all traffic from Blue (old) to Green (new) instantly. Easy rollback: just switch back.

**Canary** — Route a small percentage of traffic (5-10%) to the new version. Monitor for errors. If healthy, gradually increase to 100%.

**Recreate** — Stop all old instances, then start new ones. Simple but causes downtime. Only for non-critical services.

Interview answer: 'For critical production services, I use canary deployments — deploy to 5% of traffic, monitor error rates and latency for 15 minutes, then gradually promote to 100%. If metrics degrade, I automatically roll back. This limits the blast radius of any bad deployment.'

quiz.question: What is a canary deployment?
options: Deploying to all servers at once
Gradually routing a small percentage of traffic to the new version while monitoring
Stopping the old version before starting the new one
quiz.explanation: Canary deployment routes a small percentage of traffic (e.g., 5%) to the new version. If errors spike, you roll back before most users are affected. It's named after canaries in coal mines — early warning signals.
